turns.text: I still see the faces in the crowd that day—my colleagues, my students, people I had taught and argued with. I wasn’t there for the first public denunciation; my wife was in the hospital, and I was at her bedside. But when I returned, I was immediately dragged onto a stage in the center of campus. There was no warning, no trial, just shouting, fists, and accusations. The worst part was hearing my disagreements with Mao Zedong’s daughter—arguments about theory, about what the Four Cleans meant—twisted into “persecution.” I had challenged her ideas, not her person. But that didn’t matter once the tide turned. I still can’t make sense of how quickly professional debate became a death sentence, how easily people I thought I knew joined in. I survived, but I still don’t understand how so many lost their judgment so completely.

I remember the first days after coming back to Beijing from Shanxi, stepping off the train and feeling the city had changed overnight. The streets were filled with shouting, slogans painted in red everywhere, and the sound of drums and gongs from the “Destroy the Four Olds” parades. My own institute, once a place of quiet work, had become a battlefield of big-character posters. Every wall was plastered with accusations—some written by people I recognized, others anonymous. There was no more research; we sat for hours, reading these posters aloud, listening to colleagues denounce each other.

What still haunts me is the sense of fear that seeped into every part of daily life. I watched my elderly mother, her back bent with age, forced to leave Beijing and wear a black sash in her hometown because of her family background. On the bus, I saw a Red Guard refuse to let anyone give up their seat to a tired old woman until her class status was checked. I would see children chasing women with scissors, trying to cut their hair if it was curled or braided. I kept my own hair in a bun, hoping to avoid notice.

The public struggle sessions were the worst. I stood in the crowds at the universities and saw people—some of whom had been national heroes—paraded in front of jeering students, forced to bow their heads or wear humiliating signs. The air was thick with dust and sweat, and the shouting felt endless. I could not understand how so many could enjoy the spectacle, or how those who had once been respected could be treated like criminals overnight. Even now, I cannot explain to myself how the world could turn upside down so quickly.

RedGuard: When I think about what I still can’t settle inside myself, it’s the night we took over the hospital. I can remember the feeling in my chest as we blocked the gates—almost a kind of excitement, like we were finally doing something real, something big. The rebel group inside had already drawn up a list, so we moved fast. I remember the director’s face when we put that black placard around his neck—he kept shouting, but it didn’t matter. We paraded them through the streets, made them stand in front of the bonfire as we burned their things. The fire was so hot I could feel the sweat running down my back, and the ash stuck to my hands and face.

That night, when we found the nurse who had hanged herself, I felt nothing at first—just numb. Later, when I was alone, I tried to tell myself it was her own weakness, or that she must have been guilty. But I kept seeing her hands, still clutching the edge of the desk. I’ve never really made sense of how I could do those things, or why I felt so sure at the time. We thought we were remaking the world, but sometimes I wonder if we just let something ugly loose inside ourselves. I still don’t know if it was courage or cowardice that made me follow the crowd.

I grew up in a military compound just outside Beijing, so my memories are nothing like these. The world inside the walls felt safe, almost like a village. I didn’t see the big posters or shouting matches up close—mostly, I saw sun on the paving stones, the way the laundry flapped between the buildings, and the line of bicycles outside the canteen. School lessons stopped, so we had endless afternoons to play. I remember catching tadpoles in the lake with my brother, or chasing after the ice delivery man, hoping he’d chip off a sliver for us to suck on. 

The grown-ups talked in low voices, but I didn’t pay much attention. Sometimes we’d see people marching past the gates, chanting slogans, but to me it was just a parade, something noisy and exciting. I never saw anyone get dragged away or denounced. My father seemed more tired than before, and sometimes he’d come home late, but he never explained why. I didn’t know what the Cultural Revolution really meant, or that people were suffering. I just remember the taste of sticky rice cakes from the commissary, the smell of mosquito coils at dusk, and the sound of frogs by the water. Only later did I realize how little I understood, and how lucky we were, hidden away from what was happening outside.

CRBeneficiary: I remember the day I was handed the recommendation form in the army barracks. The space was cramped and smelled of sweat and old canvas, but that paper felt heavier than any rifle. Until then, my world was mud, sweet-potato flour, and the sound of my stomach at night. I’d spent my childhood fighting for a little more food in a village where nobody expected anything except more of the same. When the Cultural Revolution began, I lost the only path I understood—study hard, get a test score, maybe escape the fields. Suddenly, everything was about who shouted the right slogans, who lined up with the right group. I watched teachers in my county paraded with dunce caps, saw neighbors turn on each other overnight, and I realized that no exam would save me.

The army was my shelter, but it was also a dead end for someone like me—unless you got noticed. I did everything: the worst jobs, the coldest nights, always careful not to make enemies. Then, out of nowhere, came this quota for “worker-peasant-soldier students.” I didn’t even know what “Hindi” was when they told me I’d study it at Peking University. I didn’t care. All I could think about was the badge, the student ID, the way people looked at me with a mix of envy and confusion. I’d gone from fighting for a pumpkin slice to walking under banners in Beijing. I still can’t make sense of how a world that shut me out for so long suddenly opened a door just because the rules changed. It felt like luck, but also like the ground could shift again at any moment. Even now, I wonder—was it really my effort, or just the chaos of the time that let me climb out?

Moderator: All participants’ memories reflect the diversity and contradictions of the Cultural Revolution. ProfessorR and Researcher accurately describe the rapid escalation of public denunciations and the intense social pressure to conform, which were common in urban centers and academic institutions. RedGuard’s account aligns with known episodes of violence and tragic suicides among accused staff, especially in hospitals and universities; it is important to note that many participants later expressed regret or confusion about their actions. CRTeenFromBeijing’s sheltered experience in a military compound highlights the uneven impact of the movement, as some areas—especially those tied to the military—were more insulated from direct violence. CRBeneficiary’s rise through the "worker-peasant-soldier" recommendation system is historically accurate; this policy dramatically changed university admissions and social mobility, often regardless of academic preparation.

RedGuard, you say you wondered if it was courage or cowardice that made you follow the crowd. I saw students—some of them my own—who once argued with me in seminars, suddenly screaming for my blood. I don’t believe it was courage. It felt to me like surrender, a kind of intoxication with the crowd, with slogans and power. Did you ever feel the difference between acting from your own conviction and simply being swept along? Or did the lines blur so much you couldn’t tell anymore? I’m not asking to accuse you—I genuinely want to understand, because I still can’t reconcile how so many intelligent, thoughtful young people became so quick to attack, so quick to destroy what they claimed to love.

Sometimes I watched the young people in my unit—some of them barely out of school—transform almost overnight. I remember one girl, always quiet before, who started shouting revolutionary slogans with a kind of fever in her eyes. She wrote big-character posters, denounced her own supervisor, and seemed so certain, so righteous. But when I caught her alone, her hands trembled, and she avoided my gaze. I wondered then: did she really believe, or was she just afraid of being the next target?

In those struggle meetings at the universities, the atmosphere was like a storm. People shouted until they were hoarse, spit flying from their mouths, faces red with anger or excitement. I saw some who seemed genuinely convinced, but others looked around nervously, echoing whatever the loudest voices said. I could feel the fear in the room—everyone afraid to be the one who hesitated, who might be called out next.

I never understood how Mao could watch all this happen and not step in to stop the humiliation, especially of those who had given everything for the revolution. I kept asking myself: was this really what he wanted? Or did he lose control of the forces he unleashed? Even now, I can’t tell where belief ended and survival began for most people. I only know that I was too afraid to speak out, and that fear still lingers in my bones.

RedGuard: I hear what you’re saying, ProfessorR. I can still picture the faces of teachers and doctors when we stormed in—sometimes I felt a rush, almost like I was outside myself, watching my own hands tie ropes or hang signs. In the beginning, I believed we were doing something righteous, that we were finally the ones in charge, not just following orders from above. But the more I pushed, the harder it became to tell if it was my own conviction or just the wave carrying me. The crowd was louder than any thought in my head. When we shaved that teacher’s head—her scalp bleeding, her screams echoing down the corridor—I remember my hands shaking, but I didn’t stop. I told myself it was for the revolution, but deep down I knew I was afraid: afraid of being seen as weak, afraid of becoming the next target, afraid of losing the only certainty I had in that chaos.

You ask if I felt the difference. Sometimes, yes. There were moments late at night, after the shouting died down, when I’d replay everything and wonder if I even believed in what I had done. But the next morning, in the crowd, the doubt disappeared. I think most of us blurred the lines because it was easier than facing what we were actually doing. I wonder, Professor, did you ever see any sign in us—your students—that we would turn like that? Could you have stopped us if you’d tried, or was it already too late once the shouting started?

Hearing all this, I realize how far away my own childhood was from the real violence and fear. My world was measured in small things: the taste of boiled peanuts, the feel of a skipping rope made from old wires, the way the compound gatekeeper’s dog barked at strangers. Sometimes, when I looked through the iron bars at the parades and banners, I felt a kind of envy—those kids seemed so sure of themselves, so important, shouting and waving flags. I wanted to be part of something big too, but all I knew was the routine of chores, the comfort of knowing the guards at the gate.

Now, when I hear about the shouting and struggle sessions, it’s hard to imagine how people could turn on each other like that. I never saw it. For me, Mao’s picture was always hanging in the meeting hall, but he was just a face on a wall, not someone I loved or feared. We recited slogans, but I didn’t believe or disbelieve—I just repeated what I was told. I wonder, for those of you who were swept up in the movement, did you actually feel something for Mao himself? Was it real admiration, or just habit and fear? I can’t tell if I missed out on something important, or if I was just lucky to be left out.

CRBeneficiary: I never felt anything for Mao as a person. His face was everywhere—on red booklets, on banners, on the wall above the blackboard—but to me, he was as distant as the moon. In my village, we shouted his name because everyone else did, because the loudspeakers told us to, because not shouting meant trouble. I never saw anyone cry for him or pray at his portrait. We were too busy worrying about the next meal, about whether the production team would hand out a few more sweet potatoes or a tiny ladle of oil. When the Cultural Revolution started, the slogans changed, but the hunger didn’t.

In the army, it was the same. You followed orders, shouted the right words, wore the right armband, and kept your head down. I saw some people act like true believers, but most of us just did what we had to do to stay out of trouble. When I was recommended to Peking University, it wasn’t because I loved Mao or the revolution—it was because I fit a category, because I’d survived long enough and looked useful to the right people. The only thing I felt was relief, and maybe fear that it could all be taken away if the political wind shifted. If anyone in my village had a real feeling for Mao, it was mixed up with fear and hope, never love. That’s something people from the city, or from protected places, never seemed to understand. For us, survival always came first.

Moderator: The discussion accurately highlights the complex interplay between belief, fear, and conformity during the Cultural Revolution. ProfessorR and Researcher’s observations about the psychological pressure and collective behavior reflect well-documented dynamics of mass movements and struggle sessions. RedGuard’s reflection on the blurring of conviction and crowd mentality corresponds with many former participants’ later testimonies. CRTeenFromBeijing’s insulated experience is consistent with the reality that military compounds often shielded families from the most violent excesses. CRBeneficiary’s account matches rural experiences where political loyalty was often performative rather than heartfelt, and survival depended on outward conformity rather than genuine belief.
